entries.text: Last Form 5 exam done. Chem paper 2 was a disaster, I left the whole last question blank.

Everyone went to Mong Kok to celebrate and I went along but I felt empty the whole time. One year until the DSE. Everyone in my class seems to already know what they want to study and I don't even know what I'm good at. 我真係唔知自己想點。

content.title: One year to go, and no plan yet
content.headline: One year to go, and no plan yet
content.body:
Hey Kit,

Your last Form 5 exam finished this afternoon, and you left the final chem question blank. Then you went out to Mong Kok with everyone and felt empty the whole time, because the DSE is now exactly a year away and you still don't know what you want.

That emptiness is honest. It's what happens when the next big thing is close enough to feel, but not clear enough to plan for. Not knowing yet isn't the same as being behind. Most people who look sure are just louder about it.

You don't need a five-year plan tonight. You need a few slow days to breathe after exams.

Talk soon,
Your friend

Hey Kit,

You climbed Lion Rock with your cousin and, for a whole afternoon, nobody mentioned grades or the DSE. Just snacks, the view over Kowloon, and a head that finally felt quiet.

Notice where that quiet came from. It wasn't from having answers. It came from being outside, with someone easy, doing something that didn't need to be useful. After weeks of revision, your mind rested the moment it had something real in front of it.

That's worth remembering when the revision days get loud again.

Talk soon,

content.title: A report card, and other people’s plans
content.headline: A report card, and other people’s plans
content.body:
Hey Kit,

The report card came today, and the numbers weren't the ones you hoped for. Your mum went quiet and suggested a tutorial centre, your dad said medicine is still possible, and you sat there thinking you don't even want medicine. You just want to stop feeling like you're failing.

Two different things are tangled together here. One is your marks, which can move a lot in a year. The other is a future your parents are imagining for you, which might not be yours at all. Both feel heavy tonight, but only the first one is a problem to solve this summer.

The second is a conversation, and you're allowed to take your time getting ready for it.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: Four friends, four directions
content.headline: Four friends, four directions
content.body:
Hey Kit,

Hei is moving to Manchester, Ching already knows she wants law, Sam is adding Maths M2, and it feels like everyone has a plan except you.

It's easy to compare your quiet uncertainty with their clear announcements. But a plan said out loud isn't the same as a plan that works, and none of them knows yet how next year will actually feel. What's real tonight is that your group is changing, and one of your closest friends is leaving. That's a loss, not just a comparison.

It's worth marking it together while you still can.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.title: Six weeks of summer, and a question you couldn’t answer
content.headline: Six weeks of summer, and a question you couldn’t answer
content.body:
Good morning, Kit.

Your mum signed you up for six weeks at the tutorial centre, and you thanked her because you know what it costs. Then your aunt asked what you want to study at uni, you said you're not sure, and everyone looked at you.

Let's separate two things. The summer course is about the next twelve months of marks, and it's a reasonable step. The uni question is about the next ten years, and nobody should expect you to answer it at a family dinner. A short, honest line you can say without feeling judged will take a lot of pressure out of those moments.

The real answer will come from what you notice this year. Keep track of it.

All the best,
Your mentor

You saw Hei off at the airport tonight. His mum cried, he didn't, and on the bus home it hit you: Form 6 will start without him in the next seat. Then you scrolled back through your photos from Form 1.

Both things are true at once. You're losing the easy closeness of having him there every day, and you're heading into the hardest school year without your usual person. Missing him this much isn't weakness. It's what a good friendship looks like when it changes.

A message for when his plane lands keeps the thread warm.

content.headline: Eighty people, and nobody to talk to

Hey Kit,

Eighty students in one room, a star tutor on a big screen, everyone laughing at his jokes, and you ate a pineapple bun alone by the window at lunch. You came home tired from pretending to keep up.

Big rooms like that are built for listening, not for meeting anyone, so talking to nobody isn't a failure. It's what the room allows. If you want people around you this summer, you'll probably find them somewhere smaller, where there's something to do together.

So this week, look for one small group, even just two people revising the same topic.

Talk soon,
Your friend

That last line matters most. You're not alone because something is wrong with you. Before, friendship came with the timetable. This summer you have to choose a door and knock, and nobody tells you which one. That's hard for almost everyone.

Starting from something you're curious about makes the first knock easier.

content.headline: Do you actually want this?

Good morning, Kit.

A mock test today, chem at 38 again, and a break spent listening to two boys compare scores and talk about needing top grades for medicine. Then, in bed, the real question: do you want any of this, or are you doing what everyone expects?

That's a good question to ask, and you don't have to answer it under exam pressure. Here's another way to look at it. This summer, your best moments have been a photo walk, a seat saved on a minibus, and explaining titration so well that three people got it. None of them were about a score. That doesn't mean marks don't matter; it means your clues about yourself are coming from somewhere else right now.

Collect those clues for a while before you decide anything.

All the best,
Your mentor

content.title: The JUPAS question came back

Hi Kit,

It's you, a few years from now. I remember this night: first term results, chem slowly climbing, biology suddenly your best subject in years. You spent the evening reading about psychology programmes, wondering if it's silly to want that when everyone says business is safer. You were still up past midnight when you found out some unis let you combine them.

I won't tell you how JUPAS turns out, but I'll tell you what I'm glad you noticed. You weren't asking what sounds impressive. You were asking what would feel like yours. And you'd been collecting the answer for weeks without realising it: Ms Lam's book, the kids on Tuesdays, the way you light up when someone finally understands something.

You don't have to choose tonight. Find one real person who has done the combination.

With love,
You, later

Only a week ago you were wondering if wanting psychology was silly. Tonight someone showed you one way the pieces fit together, and she's only a few years ahead of you. You don't have to copy her route, but it's proof your mix of interests isn't a mistake.

Small next steps are enough. Read about one programme and see how it feels.

Talk soon,
Your friend

Hey Kit,

The last session before the kids' exams, and they made you a card thanking you for teaching them fractions. Jason drew you holding a camera. It's on your desk now, next to the photos.

Think about what that drawing means. A boy who once wouldn't even try fractions remembered both of your worlds, the tutor and the photographer. In a year when school often makes you feel behind, you became someone a nine-year-old draws. That happened one Tuesday at a time.

Keep the card where you'll see it on the harder revision days.

Talk soon,
Your friend

content.headline: You don't need the whole map yet
content.body:
Hi Kit,

It's you, a few years from now. Tonight you came home from a sunset photo walk in Kennedy Town, egg tarts and all, and wrote that six months ago you sat in Mong Kok feeling empty after your Form 5 exams. Now you have Wing, the Saturday walks and the kids on Tuesdays.

You also wrote that your chem is still not great and you don't know your JUPAS choices yet, but you know you like helping people figure things out. I want you to hear how much that is. It's a direction you found by living, not by planning: the boy at the gate, Jason and his fractions, the question you took to Ms Lam.

You don't need the whole map before the DSE. Keep following that one thread.

With love,
You, later
